# Rolling and slitting mill (`rolling_mill`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: needs gears_gear_trains, screw_nut_bolt; helped by water_wheel, puddling_wrought_iron, blast_furnace_cast_iron
- Core idea: Two hard, smooth, parallel rolls turning in opposite directions draw hot metal between them and squeeze it thinner and longer, far faster and more evenly than a hammer. The gap is set by screws at each end and reduced a little at each pass; the rolls must be thick and their housings massive, or they bend and the sheet comes out thick in the middle. Grooves cut in the rolls turn out round or square bars and later rails. In the slitting mill a second pair of shafts carrying interleaved discs cuts the rolled strip into rods for nails. Rolled plate is what boilers, tinplate and ships' hulls are made of.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thin or badly supported rolls that spring apart
  - Rolling iron too cold: it cracks at the edges and breaks the mill
  - Unequal gap at the two ends, so the strip curves
  - Fingers and clothing drawn into the nip
- History: europe: c. 1480–1500 – Leonardo draws rolls for lead and tin strip; 1550s roller mills for coin strip (Augsburg, Paris); c. 1590 slitting mill brought from the Liège region to Dartford, England; c. 1697–1728 John Hanbury rolls iron sheet for tinplate at Pontypool; 1783 Henry Cort's patent for grooved rolls; 1820 Birkinshaw's rolled wrought-iron rails; americas: 1920s – continuous wide hot-strip mill
- Read:
  - H. R. Schubert, History of the British Iron and Steel Industry from c. 450 B.C. to A.D. 1775 (1957)
  - R. F. Tylecote, A History of Metallurgy (1976)
